title: Detective Cove
blurb: Read between the lines: clues, causes and proof.

stops.title: Read Like a Detective
stops.why: Authors never tell you everything. Using clues to figure out the rest is how a story clicks, and it is a big part of every reading test.

learn.text: An inference is a smart conclusion: clues from the text plus what you already know.
Back up every inference with evidence: the exact words that gave you the idea.

story.title: The Case of the Empty Crab Pot
pages: Every morning that week, Grandpa Lou pulled his crab pot up from the dock on Kent Island. Every morning, the bait was gone and the pot was empty. "We've got a thief," he grumbled.
Maya grabbed her notebook and knelt on the muddy bank. She found tracks with five toes and webbing between them, plus a long, smooth groove sliding down into the water.
Her cousin Leo wrinkled his nose. "Smells fishy down here," he said, pointing at a pile of crab shells cracked open on a log.
That night, Maya hid behind the shed with a flashlight. Just after sunset, a sleek brown head popped out of the water, and something with whiskers slid down the bank on its belly.
Maya grinned and closed her notebook. "Case closed, Grandpa," she whispered. "Your thief is a river otter, and it really loves crab."

practice.text: Jada's sneakers are soaked and there is sand in her socks. Where has she most likely been?
practice.why: Wet shoes plus sand are clues. You know that beaches have both water and sand, so the beach is the best inference.
practice.hint: Which place has water AND sand?

how.name: Clues + What I Know
steps: List the clues the text gives you.
Add what you already know about those clues.
Pick the answer that fits every clue.
Now you try it!

practice.statement: An inference is something the author states directly in the text.
practice.why: If the author says it directly, it is stated. An inference is what YOU figure out from clues the author leaves.
practice.hint: Do you find an inference written in the text, or do you work it out?

how.name: Stated or Inferred?
steps: Ask: could I point to these exact words in the text?
If yes, it is stated. If you had to figure it out, it is an inference.
Now you try it!

practice.text: The text says: "Ben yawned and rubbed his eyes." Sort each idea.
practice.why: Yawning and rubbing his eyes are in the text. That Ben is tired, and that it might be late, are smart guesses built from those clues.
practice.hint: Can you point to the exact words? Then it is stated.

how.name: Stated or Inferred?
steps: Read each idea.
Look for those exact words in the sentence.
Found them? Stated. Figured them out? Inference.
Now you try it!

practice.text: Which TWO clues show that the dog is excited?
practice.why: A fast-wagging tail and spinning in circles are things excited dogs do. Sleeping is calm, and a blue bowl tells you nothing about feelings.
practice.hint: Which clues show lots of energy?

how.name: Weigh Each Clue
steps: Take one choice at a time.
Ask: does this clue show excitement?
Keep only the clues that fit.
Now you try it!

practice.text: Put a detective's reading steps in order.
items: Notice a clue in the text.
Connect it to what you know.
practice.why: Good detectives notice first, connect the clue to what they know, decide, and then prove it with evidence.
practice.hint: What has to happen before you can make an inference?

how.name: Detective Steps
steps: Start with what you see first.
Ask what each step needs before it can happen.
Now you try it!

practice.text: Fill in the missing word: An inference uses clues plus what you already ____.
practice.why: Inference = clues from the text + what you already know.

how.name: Remember the Formula
steps: Say the formula: clues plus ...
What do you bring to the story from your own life?
Now you try it!

questions.text: Where did Maya find the tracks?
questions.why: Page 2 says Maya knelt on the muddy bank and found tracks there.
questions.hint: Look back at the page where Maya opens her notebook.

how.name: Look Back
steps: Find the part of the story about tracks.
Read the sentence that says where she was.
Now you try it!

items: She studies tracks on the bank.
Leo spots the cracked crab shells.
She hides behind the shed at night.
She tells Grandpa who the thief is.
questions.why: Maya gathered clues by day, watched at night, and only then solved the case.
questions.hint: What did Maya do before it got dark?

how.name: Retell It
steps: Find what happened first.
Then follow the story page by page.
Now you try it!

questions.text: Why did Maya hide behind the shed?
options: to watch for the thief without scaring it away
to get out of the rain
because she was afraid of the dark
questions.why: She brought a flashlight and waited near the water at night. She wanted to see the thief, and hiding kept it from noticing her.
questions.hint: What was Maya trying to find out?

how.name: Clues + What I Know
steps: What was Maya's goal?
Why might someone hide while watching for an animal?
Pick the answer that fits both.
Now you try it!

questions.text: In the story, the word sleek most nearly means —
questions.why: A wet otter's head coming out of the water would look smooth and shiny. That is what sleek means.
questions.hint: Picture an animal's wet fur popping out of the water.

how.name: Context Clues
steps: Find the word in the story.
Read the words around it.
Try each choice in the sentence. Which makes sense?
Now you try it!

partA.text: Part A: Which words best describe Maya?

partB.text: Part B: Which detail from the story best supports your answer to Part A?
options: She found tracks with five toes and webbing between them.
Grandpa Lou pulled his crab pot up from the dock.
Her cousin Leo wrinkled his nose.
A sleek brown head popped out of the water.

questions.why: Maya studied the tracks so closely that she counted the toes and noticed the webbing. That is careful, curious detective work.
questions.hint: Which detail shows something MAYA did?

how.name: Answer, Then Prove It
steps: Answer Part A first.
For Part B, find the sentence that shows Maya acting that way.
Now you try it!

stops.title: Chain Reactions
stops.why: Everything happens for a reason. Spotting causes and effects helps you understand science, history, and every good plot twist.

learn.text: The cause is WHY something happens. The effect is WHAT happens.
One effect can cause the next thing, like dominoes falling in a line.

story.title: Why the Creek Turned Green
pages: In July, Ava noticed that the creek behind her school had turned a bright, soupy green. Her science teacher, Mr. Ortiz, said the green was algae: tiny living things that grow in water.
"After big storms, rain washes fertilizer off lawns and farms into creeks," Mr. Ortiz explained. "Fertilizer makes plants grow, so the algae grow wildly too."
The thick algae blocked sunlight from reaching the grasses growing underwater. Without light, the grasses began to die.
Baby blue crabs hide in those grasses, so fewer grasses meant fewer safe hiding spots. Ava frowned: one rainstorm had started a whole chain reaction.
That fall, Ava's class planted a rain garden of native plants by the parking lot. Now, when it storms, the garden soaks up rain before it can rush into the creek.

practice.text: Signal words help you spot a cause. Which word often signals a cause?
practice.why: Because tells you WHY something happened, so a cause usually comes right after it.
practice.hint: Which word answers the question why?

how.name: Signal Words
steps: Read each word in a sentence of your own.
Which one explains why something happened?
Now you try it!

practice.text: Two mini-stories: "The power went out, so we lit candles." "The road was icy, so the bus was late." Sort each event.
practice.why: The word so connects a cause to its effect: the power went out, SO we lit candles. The icy road made the bus late.
practice.hint: The part before so is the cause.

how.name: Why and What
steps: Ask WHY: that part is the cause.
Ask WHAT HAPPENED: that part is the effect.
Now you try it!

practice.statement: In "Since it was raining, the game was canceled," the cause is that the game was canceled.
practice.why: The rain is the cause. The game being canceled is the effect, because it happened as a result of the rain.
practice.hint: Which happened first and made the other happen?

how.name: Why and What
steps: Find the two events.
Which one made the other one happen? That is the cause.
Now you try it!

practice.text: Put this chain reaction in order.
items: His friend shared half a sandwich.
practice.why: Each event caused the next: no lunch, so hunger, so a growling stomach, so his friend shared.
practice.hint: Which event started the whole chain?

how.name: Follow the Dominoes
steps: Find the first cause.
Ask: what did that lead to? Then what did THAT lead to?
Now you try it!

practice.text: Which TWO sentences show cause and effect?
options: The dog barked, so the cat ran up a tree.
Because she practiced, Mia won the spelling bee.
practice.why: The bark made the cat run, and practice helped Mia win. The other two sentences describe things but nothing causes anything.

how.name: Signal Words
steps: Check each sentence for so, because or since.
Does one thing make another thing happen?
Now you try it!

practice.text: "The ice cream melted because it sat in the hot sun." What is the effect?
options: It sat in the hot sun.
practice.why: Melting is what happened, so it is the effect. Sitting in the hot sun is why it happened, the cause.

how.name: Why and What
steps: Find the word because.
What comes after because is the cause; the other part is the effect.
Now you try it!

questions.text: What made the creek turn green?
questions.why: Mr. Ortiz says the green was algae, tiny living things that grow in water.
questions.hint: What did Mr. Ortiz say the green was?

how.name: Look Back
steps: Go back to the first page.
Find the sentence that names the green stuff.
Now you try it!

questions.text: According to Mr. Ortiz, why did the algae grow so fast?
options: Fertilizer washed into the creek after storms.
questions.why: Rain washed fertilizer into the creek. Fertilizer makes plants grow, so the algae grew wildly.
questions.hint: What does fertilizer do to plants?

how.name: Why Did It Happen?
steps: Find what Mr. Ortiz explains.
Look for the word so: it links the cause to the effect.
Now you try it!

questions.text: Put the chain reaction in order.
items: Rain washes fertilizer into the creek.
questions.why: Each step causes the next: fertilizer feeds the algae, the algae block the light, and grasses cannot live without light.

how.name: Follow the Dominoes
steps: Find the very first cause.
Ask what it led to, again and again.
Now you try it!

questions.text: What does Ava's class most likely hope the rain garden will do?
options: help the creek, so the grasses and crabs can come back
questions.why: The garden soaks up rain before it reaches the creek. Less runoff means less algae, so the grasses and crabs get a chance to recover.
questions.hint: Think about the chain reaction. What would stopping the first step do?

how.name: Clues + What I Know
steps: What does the garden do, according to the story?
How does that connect to the chain reaction?
Now you try it!

questions.text: In the story, a chain reaction is —
options: a series of events where each one causes the next
something that happens to a bike chain
a storm that lasts a long time
questions.why: One rainstorm led to algae, which led to dying grasses, which led to fewer crab hiding spots. Each event caused the next, like links in a chain.
questions.hint: Think about how the events in the story were linked.

how.name: Context Clues
steps: Find the phrase in the story.
Read what happened just before it.
Which choice describes those events?
Now you try it!

partA.text: Part A: What happened to the underwater grasses?
options: They died because they got no sunlight.

partB.text: Part B: Which sentence from the story best supports your answer to Part A?
options: The thick algae blocked sunlight from reaching the grasses growing underwater.
Her science teacher, Mr. Ortiz, said the green was algae.
That fall, Ava's class planted a rain garden.
In July, Ava noticed that the creek had turned green.

questions.why: The story says the algae blocked the sunlight and that without light the grasses began to die.

how.name: Answer, Then Prove It
steps: Answer Part A first.
For Part B, pick the sentence that tells WHY your answer is true.
Now you try it!
